Maladaptive Strategies.value: never allow myself to feel or express anger
I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
deliberately try to leave my body or blank out

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

vignette: Forty-nine months ago, the primary load-bearing column on the seventh floor of the downtown high-rise project gave way without warning. Marcus Thorne had been securing rebar nearby when the structure groaned and sheared, trapping him beneath a drift of concrete dust and twisted steel. For three agonizing minutes, he watched through the choking gray haze as his foreman, David, was pinned beneath a collapsed scaffold. David didn't make it out. The taste of copper and drywall dust coated Marcus's tongue, and the sharp, metallic scent of hydraulic fluid from a dropped crane lingered in his throat long after the paramedics cut him free. In the weeks that followed, the event refused to settle into the past. When Marcus closed his eyes, he was immediately flooded with the same fractured, high-contrast images of David's legs trapped under the warped rebar. Those sudden, cinematic flashes were accompanied by the exact same metallic taste and the thick, greasy smell of diesel exhaust, sensations that returned with jarring specificity whenever he heard the distinct rattle of a chain hoist. The sheer, unrelenting clarity of these sensory intrusions cemented a grim certainty in him: he was fundamentally inadequate. If he had been there, watching the same sky as David, why hadn't he seen the fracture, why hadn't he stopped the collapse? The vivid memories fed his self-doubt, convincing him that his own judgment was fatally flawed and that he was utterly powerless to protect those under his watch. This conviction that his mind was broken and his judgment irreparably flawed, combined with the shattering of his belief that careful preparation and vigilance kept people safe, actively primed his brain to scan for and replay the trauma. The more he believed the world had lost all predictability and that he was to blame for its chaos, his attention locked onto the sensory fragments of the collapse, ensuring the memories returned not as passing thoughts but as persistent, inescapable recurrences. His negative appraisals acted as a magnifying glass; because he was certain bad things were inevitable and that he was inadequate, his mind fixated on the event, making the memories return with greater frequency and visceral force. To survive the crushing weight of his own inadequacy and the terror that the world was fundamentally broken, Marcus constructed a rigid defense against his own emotions. He strictly forbade himself from feeling or expressing anger, even at the men who left early, the foremen who ignored stress fractures, or the city inspectors who signed off. Channeling his energy into absolute emotional stillness felt like the only way to maintain control, but the silence only made the helplessness and shattered worldview louder, driving him to seek artificial stimulation and escape. He began betting heavily on sports and poker, chasing the brief, electric thrill of the win to counteract the numbness, and when the losses piled up or the memories grew too loud, he would deliberately try to leave his body, blanking out mid-task to distance himself from the reality of a place he no longer trusted. The sensory intrusions directly dictated his avoidance and escape behaviors on the job site. The moment the smell of fresh-cut concrete mixed with the metallic tang of welding sparks, Marcus felt that same copper taste flood his mouth. The sight of a worker suspended on a harness would instantly trigger the same fractured visual sequence of David's trapped form. Faced with these inescapable sensory echoes, his only recourse was to shut down. He would deliberately dissociate, going rigid and mentally checking out for minutes at a time, or he would rush to a nearby bar, gambling heavily just to feel something other than dread. The memories forced him into these rigid behavioral patterns because they made the present moment feel indistinguishable from the collapse. Over the months, these habits eroded his life. He avoided job sites that smelled of diesel or involved scaffolding, leaving his crew short-handed and costing him his position. At home, the emotional suppression and gambling losses created an unbridgeable distance from his ex-wife, who eventually left, citing his emotional absence. Now at thirty-nine, Marcus sits in a clinic office, his hands trembling slightly as he recounts how the constant sensory flashbacks and his belief that he is fundamentally inadequate finally made him seek help. He was terrified that without intervention, his helplessness and the shattered foundation of his worldview would continue to dictate his escape behaviors, but he is desperate for a way to stop the memories from hijacking his senses and to finally believe that he is not alone in his inadequacy.
